pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Wild, Farm & Pet Animals, ages 5–7 — the difference between WILD animals (find their own food and shelter in nature), FARM animals (kept by people for food, wool, milk or eggs) and PETS (kept for companionship) — plus the safety idea that wild animals should be observed from a distance, not approached.
• Standards — UK: DfE KS1 Y1 'Animals, including humans' (identify and name a variety of common animals) as the naming base; the wild/farm/pet grouping is a common KS1 topic framing built on that.
• Standards — US: NGSS K-ESS3-1 (relationship between organisms' needs and where they live) as background; the wild/farm/pet distinction is a human-and-animals relationship idea rather than a single PE.
• Operational details: the KEY teaching point is that these categories describe the animal's RELATIONSHIP TO PEOPLE, not a fixed property of the animal — the SAME kind of animal can be wild, farmed OR a pet (a rabbit or a pig can be a wild animal, a farm animal, or a pet), so children must reason about how the animal lives and why people keep it, not just its species; anchor a clear one-difference-each summary (wild = looks after itself; farm = kept for what it gives us; pet = kept for company); include the safety rule (observe wild animals from a distance).
• Checkpoint: [Tier A] sorts animals into wild, farm and pet categories with examples, explains one key difference for each category, and states that wild animals should be observed, not approached.
bestPractices: Foreground the big idea that the category depends on the animal's RELATIONSHIP with people, not its species — use one animal that appears in more than one category (rabbit as pet or wild; pig as farm or, in some places, wild boar) so children learn to ask 'how does it live / why is it kept?' rather than memorise a fixed label.
Give a crisp one-line difference for each group (wild = finds its own food and home; farm = kept to give us food/wool/eggs; pet = kept for company) and let children apply it as a test when sorting.
Weave in the safety message naturally: wild animals look after themselves and can be unpredictable, so we watch them from a distance and don't feed or touch them — a genuinely useful KS1 life lesson.
Use sorting with feedback and discussion of the 'it depends' cases; the productive talk is about the borderline animals, not the obvious ones.
Draw on children's own experience of pets and visits to farms/parks to ground the categories in the familiar.
keyRepresentations: A three-way sort board: WILD / FARM / PET, with a mix of clear and 'it depends' animals to place.
A one-difference-each summary card (wild = fends for itself; farm = kept for produce; pet = kept for company).
A 'same animal, different role' pairing (a rabbit shown as a wild rabbit, a farmed rabbit, and a pet rabbit) to make the relationship idea explicit.
A simple safety icon/rule: observe wild animals from a distance — look, don't touch or feed.
commonMisconceptions: Believing an animal's category is fixed by its species — not realising the SAME kind of animal can be wild, farmed or a pet depending on how it lives with people.
Thinking 'wild' means dangerous/fierce (so a wild rabbit or wild duck doesn't count as wild), rather than 'lives independently in nature'.
Assuming all farm animals are pets because they're friendly/kept by people, blurring 'kept for food/produce' with 'kept for companionship'.
Thinking wild animals in parks or gardens are tame and safe to approach or feed — missing the observe-from-a-distance safety point.
Calling any animal seen at a zoo or petting farm a 'pet', confusing where an animal is kept with the reason it is kept.

learn.summary: For ages 5–7: children learn that WILD, FARM and PET are categories about an animal's RELATIONSHIP WITH PEOPLE, not fixed labels stamped on a species. Wild animals find their own food and shelter in nature; farm animals are kept by people for food, wool, milk or eggs; pets are kept for companionship. The central insight is that the SAME kind of animal (e.g. a rabbit) can be wild, farmed OR a pet depending on how it lives with people — so children reason 'how does it live / why is it kept?' rather than memorising a label. Children also learn the safety rule: wild animals are watched from a distance — look, don't touch or feed.

activities.title: Sort the animals into Wild, Farm and Pet
feedback: If a child calls a wild rabbit or wild duck 'not wild because it isn't scary', clarify: wild means it lives on its own in nature and finds its own food and home — not that it is dangerous.
If a child puts a friendly farm animal in PET, ask: is the cow kept to give us something (milk), or just for company? Kept for produce = farm; kept for company = pet.
If a child wants to stroke or pick up a wild animal picture, remind them wild animals can be unpredictable or frightened, so we watch from a distance.
activities.rationale: Active categorisation with a stated reason builds the criterion ('how it lives / why it is kept') rather than rote species labels, and surfaces productive talk about the test itself.
learnerActions: Set out three baskets or labelled areas: WILD, FARM, PET (on paper, as cut-out pictures, or on a drag-and-drop screen with three bins).

Sort clear examples and say WHY aloud as each one is placed: fox and lion → WILD ('the fox finds its own food'); cow and sheep → FARM ('the sheep gives us wool'); goldfish and hamster → PET ('the hamster is for company').
Apply a one-line test to each animal as you sort: wild = looks after itself in nature; farm = kept to give us food/wool/milk/eggs; pet = kept for company.
When an animal lands in WILD, say the safety reminder: 'watch wild animals from a distance — look, don't touch or feed.'
activities.intendedInsight: Each category can be checked with a simple one-line rule about how the animal lives and why people keep it — not by how big, fierce or cute the animal looks.

activities.title: The same animal, three ways
feedback: If a child insists 'all the rabbits are pets because rabbits are pet animals', point to who provides the food and shelter: the hedgerow rabbit has no owner and fends for itself, so it is wild. The farm rabbit and the pet rabbit are both cared for by people, so then ask why each is kept: for meat or fur (farm) or for company (pet).
If a child gets stuck when the same animal appears twice, ask 'Who feeds this one? Who looks after it? Why is it kept?' to shift attention from species to relationship.
activities.rationale: Using one species across categories directly targets the misconception that category is fixed by species, forcing reasoning about the relationship with people.
sourceClaims: A common early misconception is that 'wild' means dangerous and that an animal's category is fixed by species; the same species can be wild, farmed or a pet depending on how it lives with people.

The relationship between organisms and the places/ways they live is a foundational early-science idea; wild/farm/pet is a relationship-to-humans distinction rather than an intrinsic property of the species.
learnerActions: Look at (or draw) the SAME animal in three situations: a rabbit hopping free in a hedgerow, a rabbit in a hutch on a farm kept for meat/fur, and a rabbit curled up as a child's pet.
Decide which is wild, which is farmed and which is a pet, and explain how you can tell them apart.

Place each of the three rabbit pictures into a basket from Activity 1 and discuss why rabbits, as a kind of animal, can go in WILD, FARM or PET. Each rabbit goes in only one basket, depending on how that rabbit lives with people.

Repeat with other 'it depends' animals: a cat (pet vs feral/living wild), a hen (farm hen kept for eggs vs a pet hen kept for company), a pig (farm pig vs feral pigs living wild in some places; wild boar are their wild relatives).
activities.intendedInsight: The category is not a property of the species; it describes the animal's relationship with people, so the same kind of animal can belong to more than one group depending on how it lives.

activities.title: Talk and check: why do we keep this animal?
feedback: If a child says you could stroke or pick up a wild deer or rabbit, explain wild animals can be unpredictable, get frightened, or carry disease, so we observe from a distance.
Reward answers that name WHO provides food/shelter and WHY the animal is kept, not just the animal's name.
activities.rationale: A light spoken or written check after sorting consolidates the one-difference-each summary and the safety rule, and the persona option adds motivating reasons for why people keep animals.
learnerActions: Answer short 'why' questions out loud or in a quick check: 'Who gives the pet rabbit its food? Who feeds the wild one?', 'Could one cat be a pet while another cat lives wild — how?', 'Is a cow wild, a farm animal, or a pet — and why?'
Answer a safety question: 'Why should we watch a wild animal from far away instead of picking it up?'
Optionally take on a farmer or vet role and explain to someone else why a particular animal is kept (for food/wool/eggs, or for company).
activities.intendedInsight: Children can state one clear difference for each group and justify a category by the animal's relationship with people, including the safety reason for keeping distance from wild animals.

constraints: Keep the big idea foregrounded: category depends on the animal's relationship with people, not its species — always include at least one 'it depends' animal that is valid in more than one group.

A tap-to-reveal scene or picture gallery (farm, home, wild wood) can serve as a reference for examples but is a scaffold only: it does not itself require the child to make the 'it depends' judgement, so pair it with active sorting and reasoning.

A fixed quiz or printed question can check sorting and the one-difference rule, but cannot easily let a child place the SAME animal in two categories; use it as a light check after hands-on sorting rather than as the main teaching.
Define 'wild' as living independently in nature (finds its own food and shelter), explicitly not as 'dangerous' or 'fierce'.
Include the safety rule whenever wild animals come up: observe from a distance, don't touch or feed; this is a look-from-afar rule, never approaching or handling the animal.
Ground the categories in children's own experience of pets and visits to farms or parks.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; all listed sources remain unverified (verified:false in the row) and were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original 3D-interactive entry claimed '3D adds nothing'; this has been dropped as a catalog-ranking judgement rather than preserved as a pedagogical law. The content is relational with no spatial dimension, which is a genuine reason a 3D model offers little here, but no universal necessity/efficacy claim is asserted.

The original framing that a static reveal or fixed quiz 'can't' teach the 'it depends' insight has been softened to a scaffold limitation (harder to represent the same-animal-two-categories case), not an absolute incapacity; neither medium is claimed to be the only way to teach the idea.
Regional accuracy note for review: the 'pig as wild boar' and 'cat as feral' examples depend on local context; present them as 'in some places' rather than as universal facts.

The KS1 naming-base source was removed from Activity 1's sourceClaims because it supports the topic/prerequisite (naming animals), not the stated pedagogical principle that active categorisation builds the sorting criterion; it remains as topic context in the summary.

Independent re-review found no new learner-facing errors, contradictions, or unsupported categorical modality claims; the two sourceClaims retained on Activity 2 are exact copies that bear on the relational-category principle the activity targets, not merely the topic.

probeDeeper: Who gives the pet rabbit its food? Who feeds the wild one?
Could a cat be both a pet AND live wild? How would that happen?
Why should we watch a wild animal from far away instead of picking it up?
Is a cow wild, a farm animal, or a pet — and why?
assess.correctAnswer: They are the same kind of animal (both rabbits). The field rabbit is wild — it finds its own food and shelter and has no owner; the hutch rabbit is a pet — a person feeds it and cares for it for company. You tell them apart by how the animal lives and its relationship with people, not by what kind of animal it is.

errorPatterns.pattern: The category is fixed by the species or by looks — 'rabbits are pets', 'lions are wild' — so the same animal can't be in two categories.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Sort the SAME animal by how it lives; add cats (pet vs feral) and horses (farm vs pet) so the child sees the category depends on the relationship with people.
errorPatterns.distractor: They're both pets, because rabbits are pet animals.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Insists both rabbits are pets, or that the field rabbit 'isn't really wild because rabbits are pets'.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Wild' means fierce or dangerous, not 'lives independently of people'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Define wild as living on its own in nature, finding its own food and shelter — not as being dangerous.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the gentle field rabbit can't be wild because it isn't scary or big.

errorPatterns.pattern: A wild animal is safe to approach if it looks friendly.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Wild animals should be watched from a distance — they can be unpredictable, get frightened, or carry disease.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says you could go and stroke or pick up the wild rabbit or a deer.

responseLevels.gap: Sorts by looks or species alone; thinks wild = dangerous; would approach a wild animal.
responseLevels.full: Sorts by the relationship with people (who provides food and shelter, and why), accepts that the same species can be wild or a pet, and knows to observe wild animals from a distance.
responseLevels.partial: Sorts common animals correctly and states a difference, but treats the category as fixed by species and gets stuck when the same animal appears as wild and as pet.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A rabbit hopping about in a field, and a rabbit in a hutch in someone's garden. Are they the same kind of animal? Which one is wild and which is a pet — and how can you tell?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Using the SAME species in two categories forces the child off 'a rabbit is a pet' (species = category) and onto the real criterion: the animal's relationship with people. A child who thinks the category is fixed by the kind of animal cannot resolve it; a child who understands wild/farm/pet as a way of living can.
